summary: Defines two new DNS resource record types for NSAP addresses and their reverse lookup, and reserves their type mnemonics and numbers. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 1637.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds two experimental record types to DNS for NSAP addresses. One record maps a DNS name to an address; the other supports looking up a name from an address.

questions: how does dns store nsap addresses
what does an nsap dns record store
subtitle: Two experimental DNS record types for storing and finding NSAP addresses.

tldr.problem: DNS needed record types for storing NSAP addresses and finding a DNS name from an NSAP address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines NSAP records to map DNS names to NSAP addresses and NSAP-PTR records for the reverse direction, with assigned type codes.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines an experimental DNS extension and updates RFCs 1034 and 1035. RFC 1637 later replaced it.

today: RFC 1348 is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 1637. It defines two DNS record types for NSAP addresses.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs NSAP Records
sections.content:
RFC 1348 defines two DNS resource-record types for representing NSAP addresses. It describes their use as a way to document addresses for static configurations of hosts and routers that use CLNP, and says they can support systems running Internet applications over CLNP.

The memo is experimental and updates the DNS specifications in RFCs 1034 and 1035.
sections.plainLanguage: The new records let DNS store addresses from the NSAP addressing scheme. The RFC focuses on documenting addresses for systems that use CLNP.

sections.title: The NSAP Record
sections.content:
The NSAP record uses type code 22. Its required fields are an owner name, time to live, class, the NSAP type mnemonic, a length, and the NSAP address. The length gives the number of octets in the address, whose format follows the assigning authority's rules.

The RFC represents the address in a master file as a character string. Its examples show DNS names paired with NSAP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: An NSAP record stores an address under a DNS name. It includes a length and the address written as a string.

sections.title: The NSAP-PTR Record
sections.content: The NSAP-PTR record uses type code 23 and provides the reverse direction: an NSAP suffix points to an owner name. The RFC describes its role as analogous to the PTR record used for IP addresses and gives examples under the nsap-in-addr.arpa name space.
sections.plainLanguage: NSAP-PTR starts with an NSAP suffix and points back to a DNS name. It provides the reverse lookup counterpart to the NSAP record.

sections.title: Status of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 1348 defines an Experimental Protocol and requests discussion and suggestions for improvement. The unit metadata records RFC 1637 as its replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes an experiment, not an Internet standard. RFC 1637 later replaced it.
